message.content:
Based on extensive research, the answer is **yes—sports can make a nation**, though with important nuances and limitations. Sports have repeatedly demonstrated their power to forge national identity, foster unity across deep divisions, and even help resolve conflicts. However, this power is contextual and not automatic.

## How Sports Build Nations

### Creating Shared National Identity

Sports serve as one of the most powerful vehicles for national identity formation. When athletes compete internationally, they become "ambassadors carrying the hopes and dreams of millions," and their victories are celebrated as national achievements rather than individual accomplishments (https://vibeblessings.com/sports-as-a-tool-for-national-unity/). The experience of cheering for a common cause allows citizens to "set aside differences in politics, religion, and identity and choose to lock arms in support of their national team" (https://www.aeaweb.org/research/nation-building-through-football-africa-cup).

Research confirms this empirically. A study in the *American Economic Review* found that Africa Cup of Nations victories corresponded with a **37 percent drop** in the probability that someone would have a strong sense of ethnic identity rather than national identity. Victories also improved attitudes toward other ethnicities and reduced inter-ethnic violence (https://www.aeaweb.org/research/nation-building-through-football-africa-cup).

### Bridging Deep Divisions

Some of the most compelling evidence comes from countries torn by conflict:

- **Ivory Coast (2006)**: After qualifying for their first World Cup, star striker Didier Drogba made a televised plea for peace during a brutal civil war. A ceasefire was announced weeks later. The team's subsequent success "was credited by many to have paved the way for a peaceful resolution of the civil war that had ravaged the country for over five years" (https://www.aeaweb.org/research/nation-building-through-football-africa-cup; https://cultureinsports.com/sports-are-the-catalyst-for-national-unity/).

- **South Africa (1995)**: The Rugby World Cup became "a symbol of national healing and reconciliation following the end of apartheid." Nelson Mandela presenting the trophy to the team "epitomized the power of sports to transcend historical divisions and promote national unity" (https://en.encyfi.com/culture-society/relationship-between-sports-and-national-identity-15327).

- **China**: The article "体育赋能铸牢中华民族共同体意识的逻辑机理" (The Logical Mechanism of Sports Empowering the Consolidation of the Chinese National Community Consciousness) describes how traditional sports festivals bring together Zhuang, Han, Miao, Yao, Dong, Mulao and other ethnic groups in shared activities—"共玩一场球、共唱一首歌、共跳一支舞、共吃一锅饭" (playing a ball game together, singing a song together, dancing together, eating from the same pot)—breaking down barriers between groups (https://www.gmw.cn/xueshu/2025-04/30/content_38002063.htm).

### Government Recognition and Strategic Use

Governments worldwide explicitly use sports for nation-building. Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu recently declared sports "a powerful tool for fostering unity among Nigerians" and "a symbol of unity" (https://guardian.ng/sport/tinubu-declares-youth-games-open-says-sports-tool-for-national-unity/). Academic research notes that "the use of sport by governments for nation building and their own legitimization is common, especially in the developing world" (https://ruor.uottawa.ca/server/api/core/bitstreams/89fe9319-50d6-4959-87ca-3a764726062f/content).

## Important Limitations and Challenges

However, sports are not a guaranteed nation-builder:

**Context matters significantly**: The researchers who studied African football noted that "the effects would [not] translate to other contexts." In the United States, for example, "those divisions were not much healed by the US Women's National Team winning the World Cup," partly because football is not as culturally central as in sub-Saharan Africa (https://www.aeaweb.org/research/nation-building-through-football-africa-cup).

**Team diversity enhances unity**: The more ethnically diverse a national team, the greater its unifying effect—suggesting that sports work best as nation-builders when they visibly demonstrate that "inter-ethnic cooperation can lead to important achievements" (https://www.aeaweb.org/research/nation-building-through-football-africa-cup).

**Commercialization threatens national connection**: When "athletes represent a multinational corporation as much as their country, the line between national pride and commercial interest can become blurred," potentially shifting motivation from representing one's country to personal financial gain (https://therealielts.vn/ielts-reading-2024-sports-on-national-identity?srsltid=AfmBOoowjdvLtg8TWT7qn7zUtKJXcmk3HrF4y6jPSFVSlb1gJTX-CIpJ).

**Sports can also divide**: "Politicization of sporting events can cause division in society instead of uniting," and intense rivalry can exacerbate tensions rather than resolve them (https://dspace.udpu.edu.ua/bitstream/123456789/18058/1/Національні_інтереси_5_5_2024%20НР.pdf).

## Conclusion

Sports **can** make a nation—by creating shared emotional experiences, providing visible symbols of collective achievement, demonstrating inter-group cooperation, and opening windows for political dialogue. However, they do so most effectively when: (1) the sport holds genuine cultural significance; (2) the national team reflects the nation's diversity; (3) commercial and political manipulation is minimized; and (4) the "Kumbaya feelings" are leveraged into concrete political opportunities. As one researcher noted, these shared experiences "may not last long, but it could potentially be enough to open a precious window of opportunity for political dialogue, negotiations, or reforms capable of producing long-lasting solutions" (https://www.aeaweb.org/research/nation-building-through-football-africa-cup).
